claims.text: TypeSafe AI opened early access to Jev, their SystemOne model, in the week before this post (September 2026).
TypeSafe's Jev provides AI primitives that let apps, agents, and workflows make decisions based on context.
Jev's decision-making primitives are confidence scoring, multiple choice, and yes/no (noul) questions.
GeoDeploy compares every AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud region that offers managed Kubernetes and provisions consistent environments across all three hyperscalers.
In GeoDeploy, the TypeScript app never makes judgment calls, Jev never does arithmetic, generates code, or invents region names, and Pulumi never decides anything.
GeoDeploy uses great-circle distance as a coverage measure for candidate regions.
GeoDeploy fetches current prices from the AWS Price List API, the Azure Retail Prices API, and the Google Cloud Billing Catalog, normalized into a single quote format.
GeoDeploy's deterministic TypeScript bin-packs pods onto nodes, filters out instance types that don't match the image's architecture, and computes a monthly cost per candidate.
GeoDeploy composes a Pulumi program from a registry of typed modules: EKS, AKS, or GKE; ECR, ACR, or Artifact Registry; ingress; DNS through Route 53, NS1, or Cloudflare; and observability.
GeoDeploy uses the Pulumi Automation API to run a preview and then an update, with one stack per region.
GeoDeploy will not provision unless cloud credentials pass readiness checks.
Every GeoDeploy run writes plan.json and plan.md with the full decision record, and a web UI shows the deployment on a live globe.
Jev returns typed answers with calibrated confidence through three primitives: choice(), score(), and noul().
Jev's choice() picks one option from a closed list and returns the pick, a probability distribution across all options, and a confidence.
GeoDeploy's score() rubrics use 10 levels.
Jev's noul() answers a yes/no question with a single probability.
Because Jev only selects from closed sets, a hallucinated region or made-up Pulumi argument cannot happen by construction.
For each geo, GeoDeploy sends Jev a shortlist of up to 40 priced candidates along with constraints and image architecture, in a single call.
GeoDeploy asks Jev for one selection, five quality scores (coverage, cost fit, maturity, sprawl risk, architecture consistency), two hard checks (residency, capacity), and a fallback region.
The file packages/decide/src/questions.ts in GeoDeploy imports choice, noul, and score from @typesafe-ai/sdk.
TypeSafe advises rubrics to 'describe situations, not degrees.'
The TypeSafe SDK exposes TypeSafeClient with a systemOne method taking state and questions and returning answers.
GeoDeploy's ranking uses weight profiles: latency-optimized (default), balanced, residency-first, and failure-domain.
GeoDeploy's weight profiles have the specific weights shown (e.g., latency-optimized: cost 0.13, coverage 0.48, maturity 0.17, sprawl 0.1, archConsistency 0.12).
In GeoDeploy, cluster and registry modules follow from the provider (AWS means EKS and ECR), leaving Jev to decide ingress posture, autoscaling posture, and node-pool sizing tier.

GeoDeploy confidence thresholds: data residency 0.95 (hard reject); new-cluster region 0.90 (top three flagged for human); existing-stack region 0.75 (keep existing); ingress/autoscaling module 0.85 (registry default); node-pool sizing 0.60 (bin-packing result); global floor 0.50 (drop AI path for that geo).
The residency check is in GeoDeploy's packages/decide/src/engine.ts.
Each AiPathAborted carries the full attempt (state, questions, and answers), so rejected answers end up in the audit trail.

If a gate check fails, the API times out or errors, or upstream is unreachable, GeoDeploy falls back to a deterministic price comparison across providers while enforcing residency and constraint checks.
The `geodeploy explain` command shows why each region won.

`geodeploy monitor` enables self-driving mode, which periodically checks each deployment's CPU utilization and asks Jev one joint question across regions with answers no-change, scale-up:<geo>, scale-down:<geo>, or shift:<from>-><to>, plus a disruption-risk check.

In self-driving mode, code rather than Jev computes node-count changes; above 0.85 confidence the resize is applied automatically, between 0.70 and 0.85 it is suggested for human approval, below 0.70 a deterministic per-region rule based on utilization is used.
CPU utilization alone is a poor autoscaling metric and is usually paired with other signals such as median request latency and error rates.
GeoDeploy is open source at github.com/pulumi/devx-geodeploy.
The link /automation/ points to a Pulumi Automation API page.
